utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Very good afternoon to everybody. May I ask Madam Registrar please to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-95-14/2-A, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And may I have the appearances for the parties. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. For the Prosecution is myself Norman Farrell, and with me is our case manager Ms. Galicia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And for the Defence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon. My name is Mitko Naumovski, attorney-at-law from Zagreb for Mr. Dario Kordic; and if the telephone lines are all right, Mr. Stephen Sayers and Mr. Turner Smith are with me also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And also -- I don't know what to say, good afternoon, when they are with you on the telephone line. I don't know what's the time is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is Stephen Sayers and Turner Smith, hearing you very well from the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning to the United States. For Mr. Cerkez, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Bozidar Kovacic appearing for Mr. Cerkez, thank you, on my own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I then ask at the same time both accused first, can you follow the proceedings in a language you understand? Are there any health problems or do you see any problems emanating from your special situation, deprived of your liberty in the United Nations Detention Unit? Mr. Kordic, please. THE APPELLANT KORDIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour, Mr. President of our Appeals Chamber. Thank you for your kindness and for your question. I can follow the proceedings, and I have no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. And Mr. Cerkez, please. THE APPELLANT CERKEZ: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I understand everything, and I have no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And just for the record, there was a meeting held yesterday under Rule 65 ter (I) read together with Rule 107. Meetings -- minutes were taken by a representative of the Registry. Thus there is no need to go into further details that what we have discussed during that meeting in preparation of today's Status Conference. This Status Conference is a follow-up of the one that took place 15th of October, 2003. Already at that time I was not that happy that I couldn't inform you on the ongoing procedures, especially being aware of your motions, setting a date for a hearing, and I think it speaks volumes that when reviewing the motions and decisions in this case, since the notice of appeal in March 2001 filed by the three parties in response to the judgement handed down the 26th of February, 2001, that time is really ripe, that we have to hear this case as soon as possible, and I'm under the impression that all parties and the Chamber, everybody wants to try his or her very best to accelerate the proceedings, and one main goal of the Status Conference is to do whatever we can to accelerate these proceedings. I already can tell you now that it is envisaged that the hearing as such takes place in the week from the 17th to the 21st of May, 2004, with the caveat that if possible, we start already the 13th and 14th of May, 2004, in case we would need to hear additional witnesses or experts, and this would facilitate the work of the parties to digest what we have heard during these hearings and then hear the final submissions the next week. So in any event, mid-May 2004. Having said this, may I ask the parties, am I correct in believing that the motions filed the 24th of January, 2003, and joined by Mr. Cerkez 28 January 2003 and Mr. Kordic's renewed motion filed on 19 September 2003 are now moot and should consequently be withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is Stephen Sayers. If I may weigh in on that. It certainly sounds like, with the schedule that the Court has outlined, that these motions are moot. The only caveat that Mr. Kordic has is, as I understand it, the Prosecution yesterday indicated that a significant quantity of new Rule 68 materials were potentially going to be disclosed to Mr. Kordic, and there was some suggestion that the last part of the delivery was going to be made to counsel shortly before the May hearing date that you've just outlined. That would be a cause of very considerable concern to us, and to the extent that the delivery of any such significant amount of new material to us three years into the appeal would an have impact upon the hearing date, we would respectfully request the right to reserve refiling the motion if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Absolutely. The question is only on the motions filed in the past. Of course, whenever you deem it necessary, you can renew the motion. I only wanted to discuss this, and already at this point in time, however, I only wanted to mention it later during this hearing. Maybe there is a kind of misunderstanding. Prosecution has indicated - correct me if I'm wrong - that they are doing, based on new material, research that can be finalised by the end of March, and it was only a request from the side of the Court that an additional research should be done and concluded by the 1st of May, that we are updated as soon as possible, taking into account that no doubt the obligation for the Prosecution to provide 68 material still stands until the final day and the judgement is handed down. So can I take it that you can agree with this proceeding?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If that question is addressed to us, Your Honour, absolutely. You can take that as agreed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I was just about to say that it is well known why the Defence of Mr. Kordic has been trying to find a way to round off our case and bring it to a conclusion, which is why we submitted our motions earlier. As for the timing of the final -- final hearing, we, in that case, would withdraw the motions we have submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I can see no objections from the side of the Prosecution. Therefore, I regard these motions as withdrawn. And before addressing the issue of the time allocated to the parties during these days in mid-May 2004, let me briefly address pending matters and motions from both parties in order to better assess the need of additional time. First a preliminary remark: We should all be aware, and it was therefore that I mentioned the huge number of motions and decisions since March 2001. A lot has happened in this Tribunal and the jurisprudence has developed. Therefore, we should do whatever we can to streamline the case, and I think it's in the interest of all parties to focus on the main issues before us instead of wasting time with already adjudicated points, points where we have now a settled jurisprudence. But let's go step-by-step. I think it was a remarkable recommendation yesterday to have a monthly status report provided by the parties in order to keep the Chamber abreast with the development, that the Chamber is aware what is the status of the disclosure, are there any intentions, concrete motions in preparation, especially on additional Rule 115 evidence. Can we, and this is only for the records, can we take it that this is so agreed by all the parties, that on each first day of the month the Chamber will receive a status report by all the parties on these matters? Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: On behalf of the Prosecution, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Naumovski, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of Mr. Kordic agrees fully. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of my client also fully agrees with this. It can only assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for your cooperation. I think it's really a good step forward. We are seized with Mr. Cerkez's Rule 150 motion of 7 April 2003, including supplemental application of 9 April 2003. This is under consideration, and we will, as soon as possible, hand down a decision on this. Taking into account the huge amount applications in these two motions, please understand that I can't already today give you an exact date when you will receive this, but we are aware that following this -- following our decision, the Prosecution will ask for the necessary time to do additional research emanating from this decision. As regards the admissibility of new -- I wouldn't say material, but I would say new submissions in relation to alleged violations of Rule Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 68, you have the decision of 11th of February, 2004 before you, and as I did yesterday, I would kindly request the parties to adhere to the time frame indicated there. That means 23 February 2004, 1200 hours, in order also to give the -- to give counsel in the United States the possibility to have these documents the very same day, and then Prosecution may respond no later than 27 February, also at high noon. We do this on purpose, this deadline of 12.00, that already before the weekend counsel not on -- yes, relatively on the other side of our globe have the chance to respond immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is Stephen Sayers. We will adhere to the schedule that Your Honour has set with respect to the February the 23rd submission. The only potential problem that we've encountered is that we checked the state of disclosures to us, and it turns out that not all of the closed-session testimony of General Blaskic has been supplied to us. We have alerted the Prosecution to this and I understand from Mr. Naumovski this morning that the Prosecution has assured the Kordic Defence that we will be receiving the omitted pages promptly; and if we do, that should obviate any problem meeting the February 23rd deadline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask, Mr. Farrell, do you want to comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday -- we were informed yesterday evening that there was apparently some pages missing. We have rectified that and worked on it all morning, and it's only 21 pages, so I can't imagine that it's going to necessarily, but I leave it to Mr. Naumovski and Mr. Sayers to review it, of course. Just one comment. I mentioned yesterday and I'd just like to reiterate for the record that the Prosecution will attempt to comply, of course, with the time frame, but in light of the fact that there's only four days for the Prosecution, and I note there's seven days for the reply but only four days for the Prosecution response, and normal proceedings, as I'm sure you're fully aware, that the responding party gets the same amount of time as the applicant. In this case it's significantly different, but we'll certainly attempt to comply. If there's any reason why we can't, I'll seek leave of the Court on that day. Otherwise, we'll be filing on the 23rd. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are fully aware that we gave two different deadlines, but there is also a reason for this, and this mainly the following, that we -- we don't and we can't expect any response from the side of the Prosecution on the merits of these new submissions. This is for the final submissions. It's only on the -- more or less on technical questions. However, when it goes to the merits of additional submissions on alleged violations of Rule 68, this has to be discussed, no doubt, during the hearing in the presence of all members of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'll certainly review the material, but I suspect that counsel for Mr. Kordic are going to address the very specific aspects of the Rule 68 and how it affects the verdict, and the Prosecution would like the opportunity to put in writing our response and not leave it, but we'll wait until we receive the filing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As I said, we only invite you to -- and request you to adhere if possible. If not possible, please let us know if there is any obstacle. Okay. As regards disclosure of 68 material, I take it that since the 15th of October, that was the date of our last Status Conference, there had been disclosure of additional 68 material, September, November, and December 2003 already. And as I already stated previously, based on new material, the Prosecution itself indicated that they wouldn't know today whether it's only a duplication of material they have already had beforehand or this is fresh material, but nevertheless, they would be able to conclude the disclosure of Rule 68 material based on the material before them and before the Prosecution now no later than 1 March 2004, and additional research would be made and concluded by the 1st of May, and then, as I said, we have to follow the Rules and no doubt they state that there is an ongoing obligation for the Prosecution until the handing down of the judgement to disclose 68 material. I think we have agreed on this, and this shouldn't cause any problems. May I now turn to the question of the appeal briefs. I repeat my invitation of yesterday to rethink in whole or in part the appeal briefs, especially in the light of the newly, and I think now settled, jurisprudence and also in the light of new facts emanating from other cases and also taking into account the approach taken by this Bench in another case and by other Bench -- Appeals Chambers' Benches and also Trial Chamber in relation to certain procedural problems. I don't want to go on purpose into details, because I want to leave it first to the parties to discuss these issues, but to give you two examples and maybe the first example is already ripe for a decision today, one of the reasons, points of appeal raised by the Prosecution, stating at the same time that this wouldn't affect the outcome of the case and the sentence, that a proof of discriminatory policy is not required under Article 5(H) of the Statute. I think this issue has become moot due to recent, and I would say now already settled, jurisprudence. Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Just as a preliminary position, I think Your Honour is correct in that regard. I'll just reserve the right to review some of the jurisprudence, but I think I can indicate now that the Prosecution will most likely be withdrawing that ground of appeal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And with a view to all our attempts to accelerate the proceedings, may I ask you to act as soon as possible, that no draft needs to be prepared and then it's just written for the paper basket. So please, as soon as possible. And it's also a very serious question for the Defence, of course. There are alleged violations of Rule 68 and the standard of review under Rule 98 bis. I think the first question is, and one has to be very precise on this, is there any prejudice? And as I already indicated yesterday, unfortunately already nine Judges have worked until now on this case, and as a matter of fairness, Judges, of course, are obliged to act immediately when they come to the conclusion that for procedural reasons there is an obstacle to proceed or a reason to send a case back to the Trial Chamber. I think you can draw the necessary inferences from the mere fact that nothing in this direction has happened until now, and you may have seen that in another case, even during appeal, that material that allegedly should have been tendered during the trial stage was accepted. Why was it accepted? Of course with a view to the fact that this may be late disclosure fuels any defective in the proceedings during trial. So therefore, also taking into account that what was said, for example, in the Stakic case in relation to the question when does a late disclosure render a trial unfair, if there is extreme high threshold, and I think that especially my learned friends in the United States know better about the high threshold for this, especially under the jurisprudence in the United States. Therefore, once again, the invitation to both parties to revisit their reasons for appeal in order to streamline, and as I said yesterday, when focusing on the core issues of the case, then it's, from my point of view, an advantage for both parties, because then the Trial Chamber is seized with the core issues only, and they can go into a more in-depth discussion of the problems before us. And in line with this is the following approach, and I appreciate that this was accepted by the parties, that the parties will not see it as a prejudice. They even will see it, regard it as an advantage if the Appeals Chamber in future will ask all parties in advance to focus in their final submissions on -- in -- on particular special points the Appeals Chamber has identified until now. I emphasise in particular on special points because no doubt each party enjoys the right also to address those special points they believe are of special importance for them. Just for -- that we have the record clear, do the parties adhere to that, what they said yesterday on this, that they will not regard this as a kind of bias on the side of Judges but see it as an advantage that the Appeals Chamber draws in particular the attention of the parties to some points? Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes. The identification of issues that the Prosecution could assist the Appeals Chamber with would be both beneficial to the appeal and also assist the Prosecution to make more focused submission, so I completely agree, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Stephen Sayers for Mr. Kordic. We completely agree that focused submissions in a case of this magnitude with a record which is so huge would be of assistance both to the Appeals Chamber and to the parties. From our perspective, we have no interest pursuing arguments which are of marginal utility. Clearly in a case of this size, all parties should be interested in focusing on only the main issues, those issues that could have the potential to be outcome determinative at the appellate stage. And of course Your Honour is quite correct, there has been a significant development in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal during the time following the filing of the last appellate briefs in this case, and Mr. Kordic will go over the brief that he's submitted very carefully and make his decisions as to those arguments that can legitimately be advanced Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and those that should be abandoned, and we will obviously inform the Appeals Chamber of our decision along those lines as soon as we can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you very much for this really valuable contribution, because I think it's -- as you said correctly, it doesn't assist the parties when they don't know where they are and more or less fishing in the fog and not knowing what is of interest, particular interest for the Trial Chamber, and therefore, we try to do our very best in preparation of the submission and no doubt this will streamline the hearings in May 2004. But also for the record, may I hear the opinion of Mr. Naumovski on this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We absolutely agree with everything that my colleague has just said, Your Honour. It is a bit difficult for us to cooperate with the distance separating us, but at any rate, Mr. Kordic's Defence, as I said yesterday, fully accepts this modus operandi that you have proposed. We will give our full cooperation, and we shall try to go through all our appellate briefs to see if there are any matters that can be resolved and need not be discussed any further. We shall in due course inform Your Honour of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And I apologise, Mr. Kovacic, that you are always second in line, but maybe you regard it as an advantage. To be serious, what about this, the suggestion that the Appeals Chamber, in writing, puts to the parties what is the particular interest where the Appeals Chamber wants to hear submissions from the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as a pragmatist by nature, I believe this is indeed in our best interest to expedite matters in this trial and reach a verdict as soon as possible. I fully agree with this approach. I can also say that I agree with any other method proposed by this very creative court, any method that will assist us in expediting the proceedings. You have effectively referred to two different issues; firstly that we are to expect guidelines from the Chamber asking specific questions and directing us to specific areas of the appeal that the Chamber deems interesting and that we need to focus upon. At the same time, I believe it refers to the second issue that we have discussed. In the light of the evolving jurisprudence of this Tribunal, the Defence should look at issues in various appeals and decide which issues to keep and which issues may have been superseded in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. In the meantime, I have nothing but absolute and unreserved support for this approach. There is, however, one detail that I would like to address which partly was addressed yesterday and to a certain degree today. I'm speaking on the basis of experience. It is my concern that sometimes we are not sufficiently able to survey all details, and some details may acquire different levels of significance under particular circumstances. We try to pare things down to what is really essential and try to avoid mistakes of that nature. If we are to make any correction to our appeal ourselves, but I also have in mind the Chamber's assistance in whittling away at this case in order to get at the points that really are essential for the sentence, it is necessary not to overlook anything that might turn out to be essential. My address is merely to say that these things need to be borne in mind. This does not necessarily happen at all times, but experience has taught me, especially at the level of appellate proceedings, some details deemed at first to be insignificant may prove to be essential eventually. As an attorney-at-law, when reviewing the appellate stage of these proceedings, I may be overly concerned about the pure mechanics of these proceedings, and I believe it needs to be stated clearly what the distinction is between the different issues, but we should nevertheless not neglect the correlation between these respective issues and the links between the issues. That's all I wish to say and I hope that my contribution will merely serve to expedite proceedings and not to make them more complicated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your valuable contributions, and I can only re-emphasise that when asking the parties to focus in their final submissions on particular specific points only, it -- of course nothing precludes any of the parties to address any of the points they have identified, and we all are human beings, and also Judges may overlook the one or other specific points and, therefore, there's no preclusion at all, and you are of course entitled to address those points you feel necessary. Okay. Then I take it it is agreed that this approach will be taken in future. And it might assist also in return if any of the parties comes across a special issue, of course addressed already in the appeal briefs, where a party believes the Trial Chamber, as such, should focus on, then please let us know that we already beforehand are aware that there might be an additional problem we have not yet identified. So far to the appeal briefs. I don't want to go into further details, only yesterday gave some hints to the parties, and no doubt it's for both parties to evaluate the risks of the mutual appeals. You're professional enough to know about this. Then let's turn now to issues related to additional evidence. I take it that the appellants, Mr. Kordic and Mr. Cerkez, have access to the material from the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case, as indicated in the last Status Conference, and I take it that emanating from this motion there will be no additional request for material under Rule 115. In its decision on application by Kordic for access to ex parte filings, Cerkez on -- I quoted this, of 17 December 2003, the Appeals Chamber did not consider itself competent to decide this issue and invited Mr. Kordic to file a motion before the Blaskic Appeals Chamber. Just for the record, may I have the most updated approach by counsel for Mr. Kordic on this issue? Mr. Naumovski, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have reviewed this, and as I told you yesterday, if we have an understanding, and I believe we did, we decided not to file this motion before a different Chamber. In addition to that, there have been no changes in relation to what I told you yesterday. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I then ask the parties, is there any intention right now to file motions for admission of additional evidence? In particular, do the parties - and this is for the planning of utmost importance - is there any intention to apply for admission additional evidence contained in Blaskic's fourth 115 motion? Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is Stephen Sayers. I know that the materials covered by the fourth motion for the admission of additional evidence filed by General Blaskic were supposed to be made available too, on Monday, this last Monday. Speaking for myself, I have not yet seen those documents, but if they are consistent with the sorts of documents that we've been given in the past, I would anticipate that there would be no additional evidence motion related to those materials filed by Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Naumovski, any additional comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps just one remark. We received these documents yesterday. We found them in our locker, and we have not managed to go through them yet, but I assume if the case is as we believe it to be, as the case has been up to now, it will be exactly as my colleague has said, and we shall not be filing any further motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. Your Honour, it is also my assumption that we shall be filing no further motions for evidence in relation to Blaskic's fourth motion for evidence, but I must say that I have not reviewed everything so far. Yesterday when we arrived in The Hague, these documents were waiting for us in our locker, the document dated the 28th of January, 2004, containing the Chamber's decision. Your order was, if I may remind you, for the parties in the Blaskic case, the OTP, and the Defence, to submit the relevant versions of their earlier motions within ten days, as well as all the relevant evidence in connection with those motions. This date, if I'm not mistaken, expired on the 9th of February, this deadline. And then you ordered the Registry to hand these documents over to us. The registry submitted all these documents to us, and that's what was waiting for us in the locker when we got here. I've managed to go through part of the documents, but the only thing we found there was those that had before been used by the OTP. That's their own submissions and their own materials, not, however, the exhibits themselves that Blaskic proposed to admit under Rule 115, which was the main objective of reviewing those documents. So what I wish to say is that we have received the best part of the documents that the Chamber's decision refers to. That was the Blaskic case Chamber decision dated 28th of January. We received some of those documents, but not the balance. What I wish to say is the following, relying on my instincts telling me what could be in those documents. If I look at the rebuttal, I see what's written there too in the OTP motion. I believe there is very little chance that this Defence could use any such new evidence, and therefore, I believe that we shall not be filing any further motions in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this regard, not as related to this particular source. I reserve the right, however, to make my final decision after I have reviewed all of the Blaskic documents. I hope that I have made myself sufficiently clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to have the transcript clear, maybe I misunderstood you. I take it that you have got all access -- at least access to all the documents that should be filed under the ruling of the Blaskic Chamber. Is this correct, or do you miss some documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not correct. There are documents missing. The Registry has only given us the documents from the OTP but not the documents that come from Blaskic himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Prosecution on this question: What is your last information?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: It's my understanding that the Prosecution and the Defence in the Blaskic case were to have filed redacted copies of the fourth 115 motion. The Prosecution filed their redacted version of the fourth to be disclosed by the Registrar, I recall it was February 6th, I think, and I understand that counsel for Mr. Blaskic filed his redacted versions, I understand, on February the 9th and thereafter there were to be copies made. It may be that there was a delay of a couple of days in the receipt of the Blaskic redacted copies, so they may have received the first set from the OTP and they received the second set. Besides the information I've just indicated, I don't have any further information, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for alerting me on this issue. And in case you have not received the missing documents by Monday, 12.00, please alert me that we can take the necessary steps that you get these documents missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your assistance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, you agree with this procedure as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let's turn to one of the most important issues, and on this -- on the outcome of the discussion now following depends how long we'll need for the hearing. That's the question. Do we need to have at all an additional witness hearing and then how many witnesses can we expect? Of course this is only a provisional statement you can give us to date, but nevertheless, I want to ask you already today and for reasons easy to be understood, I want to ask first the Defence of Mr. Cerkez. What about witness or expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may first answer the question about the expert witness. How this issue will be resolved hinges on one particular exhibit among the 160 new exhibits that I have proposed. It is a map. Should the Chamber decide that this map is sufficient, should the Chamber be satisfied that this map should be admitted as new evidence, then this would require an expert interpretation of a soldier versed in interpreting maps. In addition to new evidence, this written report by an expert witness has also been enclosed. There is a mechanism at work there, of course, and I have worked closely with the OTP to see whether the same mechanism can be applied to this case. I can't quote the Rule right now, but there is a Rule which applies during the trial itself, at least; when an expert report is submitted, the other party can accept it as it is, or they can cross-examine the expert witness. In order to try to deal with this issue along the same lines, given that we already have the expert witness, the OTP may agree to apply this Rule at this stage. If they agree, there is no difficulty at all, and we don't need to have the witness viva voce in court. As for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's just stick to this very question. I think it would be worthwhile an attempt that the Prosecution and you, Mr. Kovacic, discuss this issue together, and maybe then based on a joint motion it will facilitate the decision to be handed down by the decision -- by the Appeals Chamber on this question. May I ask both parties to give it a try to -- yeah, to -- that we have the map and at the same time some explanation of the map. If the Prosecution can live with this, then of course we can avoid hearing an expert on this. If it is the result or the assessment of that what emanates from this map can be shared by the Prosecution, I think that's the easiest way to resolve this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Assuming, of course, that it's admitted under the 115 motion. Once admitted, the Prosecution will gladly meet with Mr. Kovacic to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I want to try to put it just the other way around: That please first Prosecution and Defence of Mr. Cerkez discuss whether or not they accept, I take it, that we have already the final or the final version is already available of a military expert giving us the necessary explanation of this map, and based on this, both parties can discuss whether you would need to cross-examine based on this -- this witness and then, in a kind of package solution, the Chamber could decide on both the map and the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I appreciate the procedure. I'll most certainly speak with Mr. Kovacic about the possible procedure. I think I should make it clear the Prosecution position is that this map is irrelevant, and the Prosecution is not going to engage in a discussion for the admission of testimony and expert material which has nothing to do with the crimes for which, in the Prosecution's submission, Mr. Cerkez has been convicted. So I would respectfully submit that though we'll engage in any discussion, it will be certainly determinative if and when it's admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you, and I hope -- yeah, please, if you want to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to add something to my proposal with another solution that has to do with the proceedings but that would be technically feasible. I believe that this map meets the requests raised by my colleague, otherwise I would not be tendering it. On the other hand, there is an expert report by an expert to accompany the map, and naturally the Chamber can use this expert report when reading the map regardless of whether the witness will be heard live in court or not. I believe it is possible to have this expert report reviewed as part of the exhibit of the map, because the map can't really be used as an exhibit without this accompanying report, I must admit, for the simple reason that we people who are not well-versed in military matters are not able to read this map. If you have a map with an expert opinion attached, this map can be viewed as a legitimate exhibit. When the Chamber decides on these issues, when the Chamber reviews the question of the map, this expert report should be seen as part of the exhibit, as an integral part of the exhibit. And if the map is admitted, the expert report, too, should be admitted along with the map. On the other hand, the OTP may wish to hear the expert live if they have arguments to request that. I don't think that will be the case, because all the expert report is really about is identifying the marks used for the production of this map, and there's not much more to it than that. Thank you very much, Your Honour. I expect that you will pose further questions in connection with the other witnesses, so I will not bring these issues up myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. In conclusion in relation to this military map, I invite both parties to come together and first to discuss the relevance of this map for the convictions of Mr. Cerkez. In case you come jointly to the conclusion that it's not relevant, then I would expect a joint response to this stating that it might not be or is not relevant. However, if you come to the conclusion jointly that the map as such is relevant, then I would expect from both parties a submission whether or not in addition to the map as such, read in conjunction with the expert report, the Prosecution wants to cross-examine the witness. I think we can live with this two-step approach. I can't see objections, so please --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Excuse me. I apologise for interrupting. There is a third scenario, which is that we don't agree. The first is that we both agree it is irrelevant and the second is we both agree it is relevant. I think our filings, as I'm sure you're fully conversant with them, make it fairly clear that counsel for Mr. Cerkez has indicated that he sees the map as relevant to the issue as to where the ABiH forces were. As I'm sure you're aware, the Prosecution's position is that unless that somehow exonerates Mr. Cerkez in some type of defence in that he was engaged in lawful military activity, the map as to where the ABiH forces are is irrelevant, and that's the subject of the dispute in the 115 motion. I'm certainly willing to go back and look at it again at Your Honour's request; but if the third option arises, which is that we can't agree whether it's relevant or irrelevant jointly, we'll also inform you of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this, the Chamber knows where we are and what we have to do. Let's turn now to the witnesses as such. The Defence of Mr. Kordic. Is there any intention to hear additional witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Stephen Sayers, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, I listen to the United States first, as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The answer is no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I take it that also the answer of Mr. Naumovski is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I can only confirm what I said yesterday. We have looked at everything that we've had in our possession up to this very day, and we don't think we will be requiring any further witnesses. There is still a theoretical possibility that we change our mind after we've reviewed new documents, but this is not very likely. This doesn't seem very likely at the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to thank you, both counsel in the United States and Mr. Naumovski. Now Mr. Kovacic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I also don't think so, but we have to look at the Blaskic evidentiary hearing and the related documents. I have now received the confidential witnesses. These have kindly been disclosed to us by the OTP. And then perhaps based on that, but I believe personally that the likelihood of anything like that happening is indeed very small. At any rate, should the need arise for that, I will immediately inform the Chamber of the possibility. That means even before filing a possible motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I appreciate very much this approach, and it is therefore that I do not intend at least to try to set any deadlines because it could destroy the spirit of mutual cooperation as we can feel it now in this courtroom, and therefore, I take it then whenever a change may happen, the parties will inform the Chamber immediately, that we can act with a flexible response. But I should not forget to ask the Prosecution, what about other witnesses for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, as indicated yesterday, the Prosecution is considering the possibility. At this point in time I'm not at liberty to indicate whether the Prosecution will call or -- I'm sorry, will seek the Court's permission to call evidence. There's two aspects to that. The first is whether the Prosecution intends to bring any other witnesses that are presently not before the Kordic Chamber. And secondly, whether, as a result of the additional evidence admitted, the Prosecution would consider it necessary to call any witnesses in rebuttal. In relation to the second issue, the rebuttal, I can't say now because I don't know which and if any material will be admitted, but depending on what evidence will be admitted, of course we will inform the Chamber after that decision. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And I take it from our discussion yesterday, that in all likelihood there wouldn't be more than three - of course things can change - more than three witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: At the moment it would be a limited number, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then it's also for technical reasons for the Defence to decide what you present or you still want to present as additional evidence because presenting new evidence opens doors for rebuttal evidence, and so forth. It's in your own hands what we will hear or what we will not hear. You should be aware of this. We are in an extremely difficult situation because we are confronted with three appeals, and there is no doubt an interrelationship between all these appeals, and of course the technical procedure is of importance. But I need not tell you this. You know better than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I briefly respond to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- the points that Mr. Farrell raised, the two points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell indicated that there was a possibility of calling witnesses in rebuttal. Obviously he is entitled to do that. There was some suggestion, however, that he might be making a motion to call additional witnesses for some other purpose or in some other context. Presumably that would be within the context of Rule 115, and if that is the case, then our position would most affirmatively be that the Prosecution does not have the right to do that. The Defence was ordered to file their Rule 115 motions, if they saw fit to do so, in April of 2003, and under elementary principles of the equality of arms, it would not be right or appropriate for the Prosecution to be seeking to be making Rule 115 motions at this very late stage of the game.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please understand that I don't appreciate to use the word "game" in the context of criminal proceedings, but maybe this may emanate from difference in culture and we have to live together coming from different cultures. Of course the -- when deciding on additional evidence, especially on additional witnesses, the Chamber has to take into account first when it would be a fresh witness whether to allow any new 115 submission, and then of course there are limits given by the appeal briefs, and I have no doubt the Prosecution is aware of this. And second, rebuttal, it's for you whether you open the doors for rebuttal evidence or not, but you will take this into account, I have no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, please forgive my unfortunate metaphor. A more appropriate way to say it would be at this late stage of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification. And having heard this, this encouraging approach of all of the parties, I think it wouldn't be appropriate to allocate already today hours for the final submissions of the parties. We have discussed certain frameworks yesterday. However, it might be that in light of the discussion of yesterday and today, the hearing can be substantially shortened and it would be premature already today to allocate hours for the final submissions. So let's wait what finally will be admitted by the entire Chamber as additional evidence. May I ask the parties, are there any other issues to be addressed today in the framework of this Status Conference?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nothing new, Your Honour, but if I just may be given an opportunity, I would like to go back to what you said a moment ago about rebuttal evidence. It appears that we are two parties in these proceedings, but actually after the Cerkez Defence have filed their 115 motion, we are three parties. So we just wish to draw the Chamber's attention to our position in view of some documents that have been proposed for admission, and hereby I mean also that some of our rights should be borne in mind that we might decide to exercise should the need arise. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Absolutely. We are discussing individual criminal responsibility and, therefore, each person has to be treated individually and no doubt we have to make a clear distinction whatever comes from your -- from both sides, from both appellants to my right-hand side. May I ask finally, Mr. Kovacic, is there anything else you want to address today? Please, I already now wanted to alert the parties that immediately after this Status Conference an ex parte and confidential hearing will take place in the presence of the Defence and Mr. Cerkez only. It is based on a justified ex parte motion, and an ex parte decision that has absolutely nothing to do with any of the other parties. We have to discuss whether in the -- in the Bench, in the framework of the Bench, whether or not we have to hear the Prosecution on this, but it's absolutely a private and very personal interest of Mr. Cerkez we will address when we have concluded this Status Conference, and therefore, after a break, we will later continue with this issue, and therefore, before giving you the floor, I wanted to address this that you don't feel the need to address this already now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. As far as this Status Conference is concerned, I have nothing further to add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank all the participants of these hearings for their constructive approach, and also my thanks go to my learned friends in the United States, and I want to conclude once again by saying what I said already yesterday: I personally invite the parties come together and to mutually exchange their views on the inherent risks when proceeding with the respective appeals, and I don't want to go one step further than this, but saying that it stays true what I said yesterday, if there is any point that can be settled in the presence of the Judge, please feel free to contact the Chamber and we will assist you. And I take it that based on our discussion, we will -- you will inform us as soon as possible. And in addition to this, each first day of each month - this is now March, April, and May - we will get a kind of status report, and if need may be, we convene another Status Conference before the appeals hearing. I hereby declare this Status Conference adjourned, and we will proceed, as I told you beforehand, in ten minutes.
